Alarm
uh-LARM
n.
From the Italian all' arme, to arms. Webster 1828: any sound, outcry or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a summons to arms. In the Authorized Version the alarm is a specific trumpet signal, distinguished by God Himself from the ordinary call to assemble.

Biblical Definition

God gave Israel two silver trumpets and two signals, and He distinguished them. When ye blow an alarm, then the camps that lie on the east parts shall go forward (Numbers 10:5); when ye blow an alarm the second time, then the camps that lie on the south side shall take their journey (Numbers 10:6). Then the crucial verse: But when the congregation is to be gathered together, ye shall blow, but ye shall not sound an alarm (Numbers 10:7). The same instrument, played two ways, calls a people to move out or to come in, and the difference is not left to the trumpeter’s taste. The prophets take the alarm as the sound of the day of the LORD. Jeremiah cannot bear it: my heart maketh a noise in me; I cannot hold my peace, because thou hast heard, O my soul, the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war (Jeremiah 4:19). Joel makes it the summons to repentance: Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the LORD cometh (Joel 2:1). Zephaniah names the day itself a day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities, and against the high towers (Zephaniah 1:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ALARM as any sound, outcry or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a summons to arms; and the sudden fear or apprehension excited by such notice.

expand to see more

ALARM, n. [It. all' arme, to arms.] — Any sound, outcry or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; as, to sound an alarm.

A summons to arms; the call by which men are aroused to defence.

Sudden surprise with fear or terror; also, terror; a sensation excited by an apprehension of danger.

The Italian origin is a shouted command, and that is the biblical function. An alarm is not an atmosphere of anxiety; it is a signal with a specified meaning that requires a specified response.

Key Scripture

Numbers 10:5 — "When ye blow an alarm, then the camps that lie on the east parts shall go forward."

Numbers 10:6 — "When ye blow an alarm the second time, then the camps that lie on the south side shall take their journey: they shall blow an alarm for their journeys."

Numbers 10:7 — "But when the congregation is to be gathered together, ye shall blow, but ye shall not sound an alarm."

Jeremiah 4:19 — "My bowels, my bowels! I am pained at my very heart; my heart maketh a noise in me; I cannot hold my peace, because thou hast heard, O my soul, the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war."

Joel 2:1 — "Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the LORD cometh, for it is nigh at hand;"

Modern Corruption

The alarm is corrupted in two ways: by pulpits that never sound one, so that the day of the LORD is announced to nobody; and by ministries that sound nothing else, so that a congregation is kept perpetually agitated and learns to ignore the trumpet.

expand to see more

Numbers 10:7 is a rebuke to the second error before it is a rebuke to the first. When the congregation is merely to be gathered, ye shall blow, but ye shall not sound an alarm. God distinguishes between calling His people together and calling them to war, and He forbids using the war signal for the ordinary summons. A ministry that treats every issue as an emergency, every cultural development as the last crisis, and every sermon as a call to arms has broken this ordinance, and the practical result is that when a real alarm comes the camp does not move. Paul makes the same point about clarity: if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle? (1 Corinthians 14:8).

The opposite failure is the more common in comfortable churches. Joel 2:1 commands the alarm precisely because the day of the LORD is at hand, and the chapter goes on to the great call, turn ye even to me with all your heart, with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning. Jeremiah 4:19 shows what it costs a man to be the trumpet: he is pained at his very heart and cannot hold his peace. A preacher who has never felt that has probably never sounded it. Ezekiel sets the watchman’s duty and the penalty for silence side by side — if the watchman sees the sword come and blows not the trumpet, the people’s blood is required at his hand (Ezekiel 33:6).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew terua' is a shout or blast, the same noun used of the shout at Jericho and of the joyful blast on the day of the trumpets; its verb means to raise a shout.

expand to see more

Hebrew terua' (H8643) — a shout, blast, alarm; the trumpet signal of Numbers 10:5-7 and the sound of Joel 2:1.

Hebrew rua' (H7321) — to raise a shout, to sound an alarm; the verb behind the noun, and the shout at Jericho.

Hebrew chatsotserah (H2689) — the silver trumpet of Numbers 10, distinct from the ram’s-horn shophar.

Hebrew yom terua' — the day of blowing of trumpets (Numbers 29:1), where the same noun names a feast rather than a warning.

Greek salpigx (G4536) — a trumpet; behind if the trumpet give an uncertain sound (1 Corinthians 14:8) and the last trump of 1 Corinthians 15:52.

Usage

"When ye blow an alarm, then the camps… shall go forward (Numbers 10:5) — a signal with a fixed meaning and a required response."

"Ye shall blow, but ye shall not sound an alarm (Numbers 10:7) — God forbids using the war signal for the ordinary summons."

"Sound an alarm in my holy mountain: for the day of the LORD cometh (Joel 2:1) — the alarm as a call to national repentance."
